options: The diff should be computed against the base branch rather than since the last round, because carried questions need the full change as context.

A pending session is carried forward as unanswered even if its author already submitted answers; those answers should be graded first, so the new round does not ask them again and the results are posted.
Questions of a pending session should not be carried at all; each push should ask only about its own diff.
The pending session should be discarded when a new push arrives, so that stale questions about the old head never reach the author.
MultipleChoice.prompt: This simplified code starts a new round when a push arrives on a pull request. Soqrates asks questions about each push, carries over unanswered ones, and grades answers once the author submits them. The grading run is separate and can lag behind a push. One line is subtly wrong for the case where the author submitted answers to the latest round just before the push. Which line is it, and why is it a bug?
reasons: Asking about only the change since the latest round is a deliberate way to avoid repeated questions. It has nothing to do with answers that were submitted but never graded.

A push can land before the run that grades submitted answers. The session is then still pending, and carrying it blindly discards the author's answers and repeats questions they already answered. Submitted answers by the author must be graded before the new round is composed, and only unsubmitted ones carried.
Carrying unanswered questions is intended: otherwise a push could make pending questions disappear and let the author skip them. The bug is carrying questions whose answers were already submitted.
Discarding would also silently drop questions the author has not answered yet, and would lose any submitted answers. Pending questions should stay until answered.

questions.explanation: A push can land before the run that grades submitted answers. The session is then still pending, and carrying it blindly discards the author's answers and repeats questions they already answered. Submitted answers by the author must be graded before the new round is composed, and only unsubmitted ones carried.

options: The comment is not graded. It is a near miss because the first word is an accepted prefix but the verb is misspelled, so the forge replies with a hint. If the author posts the same text again, they get no second hint.
The comment is graded as an answer. Both `/socrates` and a one-typo verb are tolerated, so the first question is recorded as option a.
The comment is rejected and the author gets a hint on every repost, so that they keep being reminded until they fix it.
The comment is ignored silently, as it would be if it were ordinary chat, because only an exact `answer` verb is recognised.
MultipleChoice.prompt: A pull request has an open Soqrates session. The author posts a comment whose first line is `/socrates anwser`. The next line is `1. a`. What happens?
reasons: The first word is valid and the verb is not, so it is a near miss. Near misses are never graded, get a hint, and the same text is not hinted twice. The aim is to correct a typo once without spamming the thread.

Forgiveness covers the `/socrates` spelling, letter case and the app mention. It does not cover a misspelled verb, so the verb must match `answer` exactly, ignoring case. Grading a mistyped command would also risk grading comments that were never meant as answers.
Hints are deduplicated: an identical near-miss comment that has already been hinted gets no new hint. Repeating the same hint would add noise without adding information.

Silent ignoring is how a comment that is not addressed to Soqrates is treated. A comment that starts with a prefix close to the command is deliberately classed as a near miss, so the author learns why nothing happened.

questions.explanation: The first word is valid and the verb is not, so it is a near miss. Near misses are never graded, get a hint, and the same text is not hinted twice. The aim is to correct a typo once without spamming the thread.

options: Putting the functions in a struct makes them run concurrently. The borrowed references let the async steps be polled in parallel instead of one after another.
The `impl` block lets the compiler infer the bounds from the field types. The `where` clause is documentation only and could be dropped without changing behaviour.
The struct needs the bounds to be constructible. Without them, `CiCheck { app, scm, code }` would not compile, so the `impl` bounds duplicate a requirement the struct already enforces.
The struct owns the app, the forge and the code source. Each run of the check therefore gets its own copies, so the bounds no longer have to hold for the originals.

The one `impl` block with its `where` clause gives every method the trait bounds on the type parameters. Each step can call trait methods through `self.app`, `self.scm` and `self.code` without restating the bounds, and the struct only holds shared references.
MultipleChoice.prompt: In the author's change, the free async workflow functions that each repeated the long generic bounds became methods in one `impl` block on a small struct holding references, shown in the hunk. What does this structure achieve, and why does it work?
reasons: Moving async functions into methods does not change how they are scheduled. They still run sequentially when awaited in turn, and the refactor only removes repeated bounds and parameters.

Rust does not infer trait bounds on a type parameter from its use in fields. Without the `where` clause, calls such as `self.scm.pull_request(pr)` would fail to compile because the type is not known to implement the trait.
The struct declaration has no bounds, and a struct can be built with unbounded parameters. The bounds are needed only where trait methods are called, which is the `impl` block.
The fields are shared references with the lifetime `'a`, so nothing is copied or moved. The caller still owns the values, and the bounds must hold for their types.

The bounds are written once on the `impl`, so every method inside it is checked under them. The struct borrows its three inputs, so methods reach them through `self` instead of taking them as separate parameters.

questions.explanation: The bounds are written once on the `impl`, so every method inside it is checked under them. The struct borrows its three inputs, so methods reach them through `self` instead of taking them as separate parameters.

options: It prints 2, because all `impl` blocks of one type share the type's private methods wherever they are written.
It does not compile: `router` is private to the `engine` module, so the sibling `grading` module cannot call it, even from an `impl` of the same type.
It does not compile: `grade` is `pub`, but `Engine` is imported through `super`, which hides its methods.
It does not compile: an inherent `impl` for a type must be in the module that defines the type.
MultipleChoice.prompt: A large engine type is split so that each use case lives in its own sibling module with its own `impl` block, as in the snippet. The struct and a helper method that returns the stores router stay in the `engine` module, and the helper has no visibility modifier. What happens when this crate is built and run?
reasons: This assumes privacy is per type. It is per module, so the call to `router` from the sibling module is rejected and the program never runs.

Privacy follows the module where an item is defined, not the type it belongs to. A private method is visible only in `engine` and its descendants. Giving it `pub(super)` makes it visible to the parent and so to sibling modules, which is how a facade split into sibling `impl` blocks can share a router accessor.

Importing a type with `use super::engine::Engine` brings in the type and its visible methods, and `grade` is added by the new block. Nothing is hidden by the import path. Only the private `router` call fails.
Inherent `impl` blocks can be placed in any module of the same crate. The error here comes from the private method's visibility, not from where the block sits.

questions.explanation: Privacy follows the module where an item is defined, not the type it belongs to. A private method is visible only in `engine` and its descendants. Giving it `pub(super)` makes it visible to the parent and so to sibling modules, which is how a facade split into sibling `impl` blocks can share a router accessor.

options: The state is computed once by a single query, so the order of lookups and the "absent" case are decided in one place. The exhaustive `match` makes the compiler force every caller to handle each state, including being-graded, and a new state would not compile until it is handled.
An enum with a `match` is needed because Rust cannot run several async lookups one after another. A single call that returns one value avoids that limitation.
The `match` runs the lookups lazily, so it avoids querying the graded record when the session is still pending. A series of separate calls would query every store each time.
The `Absent` arm could be dropped, because a wildcard arm in the `match` would behave the same way and keep the code shorter. Exhaustiveness only matters for style.
MultipleChoice.prompt: In this change, `report` calls `session_state(key)` once and matches on the returned enum. It does not call separate lookups for a pending, a being-graded and a graded session. Why is this design better for the correctness of the code?
reasons: The enum puts the lifecycle rules in one function. A caller can't forget a state such as `Grading`, which would otherwise risk opening a new session for a key that is already being graded. Adding a variant later turns into a compile error at every exhaustive match.
Rust can await several lookups in sequence without trouble. The enum is about modelling the states and putting the ordering in one place, not about an async limit.

The laziness comes from `session_state` returning early, not from the caller's `match`. Separate calls could short-circuit too. The enum's value is that the states are explicit and handled exhaustively.

A wildcard arm would silently absorb any state added later, such as a new lifecycle variant. That removes the compile-time check that every state has been considered, which is the point of an exhaustive match. Exhaustiveness is a safety property, not a style one.

questions.explanation: The enum puts the lifecycle rules in one function. A caller can't forget a state such as `Grading`, which would otherwise risk opening a new session for a key that is already being graded. Adding a variant later turns into a compile error at every exhaustive match.
